item.title: Driving license in Freiburg: conversion and exams
item.description: Procedure for converting a foreign driver's license in the Canton of Freiburg: compulsory courses, theoretical and practical exams, required documents and step-by-step roadmaps.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The foreign license is not automatically valid: it requires cantonal conversion - Mandatory procedure: courses, theoretical exam, practical exam - Competent authority: Office of the circulation of the Canton of Fribourg - Times and costs vary; consult the local office
## Key facts - **What**: Conversion of foreign license in the Canton of Fribourg - Who: Office of the circulation of the Canton of Fribourg - Where: Canton of Fribourg, Switzerland - When: From arrival and registration of residence - Legal level: Cantonal ordinances on road traffic - Mandatory components: Courses, theoretical exam, practical exam
The driving license is an essential document for those residing or working in Switzerland. If you arrive in the Canton of Fribourg with a driving license issued by a foreign country — whether it is a country of the European Union, a third country, or a different Swiss canton — you will quickly discover that it is not automatically recognized for driving in the Fribourg territory.
The reason is simple: in Switzerland, the competencies on road traffic, driving licenses, exams, and conversions of foreign licenses fall under cantonal jurisdiction. There is no "national" Swiss license; each canton manages its own license system according to specific cantonal ordinances. Fribourg is no exception. The Canton has developed its own process for the conversion of foreign licenses, which includes a series of preparatory courses, a theoretical exam on road signs and Swiss regulations, and a practical driving exam. These are not optional.
### Who is responsible and where to go
The Office of the circulation of the Canton of Fribourg is the competent institution for all matters related to driving licenses, conversions, renewals, and administrative sanctions. It is at this office that you must submit an application for conversion, provide the required documents, enroll in courses, and book exams. Contacting the circulation office directly is the first mandatory step: you can receive information on processing times, administrative fees, available courses, and exam dates.
Even if you come from a member country of the European Union, with which Switzerland has free movement agreements, your license is not automatically valid permanently in the canton of Fribourg. Technical standards, road signs, and traffic codes can differ significantly; the conversion ensures that you actually know the local rules and can drive safely on Swiss alpine and urban roads. ## The three pillars of conversion: courses, theoretical exam, practical exam
The procedure for converting a foreign licence in the Canton of Freiburg is divided into three distinct and mandatory phases, each with a specific purpose.
** Compulsory preparatory courses ** Before taking the exams, the applicant must attend preparation courses organised by bodies authorised by the canton. The courses address specific topics of the Swiss and Freiburg reality: Swiss road signs, speed limits, rules of conduct on mountain roads, vehicle equipment obligations (winter chains, danger triangles, high-visibility vests), and road safety regulations. These courses are not optional; their attendance is a necessary condition to access the official exams.
Theoretical examination The theoretical examination tests knowledge of Swiss and cantonal road traffic regulations. It is generally conducted in written or digital form, with multiple-choice questions. It covers the international signs adopted by Switzerland, the road code, correct behaviour in critical situations (fog, snowfall, aquaplaning), specific driving rules on alpine passes, and other aspects of Swiss roads. Passing this exam is a prerequisite to access the practical exam.
Practical exam After passing the theoretical examination, the applicant takes a practical driving test with an official examiner from the canton.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## How to proceed: the practical roadmap in 7 steps
Step 1: Contact the traffic office The first step is to submit an official conversion request to the traffic office of the Canton of Fribourg. You can contact them in person at their headquarters, by letter, or through the canton's online portal (if available). The office will provide you with the complete list of required documents, the administrative fees to be paid, and an indicative calendar of available courses. Do not hesitate to ask specific questions about timing and costs.
Step 2: Gather documents and pay fees Prepare all required documents: foreign driver's license, identity document, proof of residence. Pay the administrative fees set by the canton to the traffic office (amount not yet specified; verify with the office). This step is a prerequisite for enrolling in courses. Keep payment receipts and document submission certifications for future reference.
Step 3: Enroll in preparation courses The traffic office provides a list of authorized entities offering preparation courses. Choose the provider and date that suits you best, and formally enroll. Courses may be offered in Italian, French, or German, depending on the provider. Confirm the start date, duration, and documentation required for attendance.
Step 4: Attend courses and obtain the certificate Participate in all mandatory courses and obtain the official attendance certificate. This certificate is required to book the theoretical exam. Do not miss classes; absence may require repeating the entire course.
Step 5: Book and take the theoretical exam Once you have received the attendance certificate, contact the traffic office to book the theoretical exam. The date will be assigned according to the office's availability. Study Swiss regulations well before the exam. If you pass the theoretical exam, you can proceed to the next step; if you fail, you can retake it within the allowed number of attempts.
Step 6: Book and take the practical exam After passing the theoretical exam, you can book the practical driving exam. Dates are subject to availability. The exam is conducted with a vehicle provided by the office or, in some cases, with your private vehicle (if it meets cantonal standards). Practice driving on Swiss roads before the exam.
Step 7: Pick up the converted driver's license If you pass both exams, the traffic office will issue the converted driver's license, valid in the Canton of Fribourg and throughout Switzerland. Verify that the data on the license is correct before leaving. The license will be valid according to Swiss federal regulations.
### Variable Times and Operational Support The overall duration depends on variable factors: processing times of the traffic office (which vary seasonally), availability of preparation courses, speed at which you complete the courses, availability of exam slots, and results of exam attempts. If you fail an exam, the time increases for a retake. Report your timing needs to the traffic office (e.g., if you need to drive for work as soon as possible) — sometimes it is possible to speed up the process.
For those who need to calculate an overall budget for the conversion procedure, or wish to understand how obtaining the Fribourg license impacts car insurance and tax planning, you can use the [salary and cost calculator](nav:calculator) to explore operational spending scenarios.
Final checklist for monitoring: - Conversion request submitted to the traffic office? ✓ - Documents gathered and administrative fees paid? ✓ - Enrollment in preparation courses confirmed? ✓ - Attendance certificate received? ✓ - Theoretical exam passed on the first attempt? ✓ - Practical exam passed? ✓ - Converted license picked up and verified for data accuracy? ✓

item.description: Complete guide to security deposit, fee dispute and cancellation according to the Federal Bond Code. Conciliation procedure and deadlines.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Security deposit: up to 3 months' rent in a blocked account - Rent dispute: within 30 days to the conciliation authority - Landlord's notice: cantonal form with 1/2/3 months' notice - Tenancy law: federal, identical in all cantons
## Key facts - **What**: Security deposit and tenant rights - Where: Canton of Fribourg (federal law CO art. 253 ff.) - Who: Tenants, landlords, cantonal conciliation authority - Amount: Up to 3 months' rent - Deadline: 30 days for conciliation appeal - Form: Notice only on official cantonal form - Competence: Swiss federal Code of Obligations
Tenancy law in Switzerland follows uniform federal rules codified in articles 253 and following of the Code of Obligations. In the canton of Fribourg, as in every Swiss canton, tenants and landlords operate under identical federal rules. This means that the rights of dispute, notice procedures, and management of the security deposit remain unchanged, regardless of the geographical region.
One of the most frequent issues concerns the security deposit. Federal law stipulates that the security deposit may not exceed three months' rent. It must be paid into a blocked bank account in the tenant's name only. The landlord may not use it except to offset certified amounts due or documented damages. If the deposit requested exceeds three months, the tenant has the right to contest it within specific deadlines.
A second critical aspect is the dispute of the initial rent. If the tenant believes the rent is excessive compared to local standards, they have 30 days to appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority for tenancy matters. This authority acts as the first instance of dispute resolution and can order a rent reduction if it finds a disproportion compared to local rents.
Notice represents another frequent area of conflict. The landlord can terminate the contract only by using the official cantonal form and respecting the notice periods: one month during the first year, two months from the second to the ninth year, and three months from the tenth year of occupancy. A notice drafted differently from the official form is null and void. ### Conciliation procedure in case of dispute
The cantonal conciliation authority in rental matters is the first competent body to resolve disputes between tenants and landlords. When a tenant disputes the initial rent, they have 30 days from receipt of the contract to file an appeal. The deadline is peremptory: after 30 days, the dispute is no longer admissible according to the Federal Code of Obligations. The conciliation authority examines whether the proposed rent complies with the parameters of reasonableness and conformity with the standards of the area. If the appeal is accepted, the authority can order a reduction in rent and reimbursement of the excess amounts already paid by the tenant.
The security deposit can also be disputed according to the same procedure. If the landlord requests a deposit exceeding three months' rent, the tenant can appeal to the conciliation authority within 30 days of the request. There are no appeal costs for the tenant; the procedure is simplified compared to an ordinary civil trial. The conciliation authority operates based on the Federal Code of Obligations, and its decisions can be appealed to the cantonal civil court within further established deadlines.
### The blocked account: protection of the tenant
The security deposit must be paid into a separate blocked bank account, solely in the tenant's name. This protection is fundamental: it prevents the landlord from accessing the funds for other purposes or using them as compensation for rents not yet due. During the lease, the money remains blocked. The landlord can only withdraw from the deposit if there are certified credits (documented outstanding rents or proven material damages) and must communicate in writing to the tenant the amount withdrawn, the reason, and the supporting documentation. At the end of the lease, the landlord has the obligation to return the deposit increased by the accrued interest, deducting only the legitimately due amounts. If the landlord unjustly withholds the return or does not comply with the return deadlines, the tenant can take legal action to obtain the amount plus moral damages.
### Termination: variable terms and nullity
The termination of the lease contract must be communicated in writing using exclusively the official cantonal form. No other form is legally accepted. An email, a personalized letter without the official form, or a verbal communication DOES NOT constitute a valid termination according to the Code of Obligations. The notice periods vary according to the seniority of the lease: one month for the first year, two months from the second to the ninth year, three months from the tenth year onwards. These terms are non-derogable and codified in federal law. A termination lacking the exact date, the original signature, or completed with the wrong form is null. The tenant can challenge it with the conciliation authority within 30 days of receipt and request the annulment of the termination.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ### Checklist for new tenants in Fribourg
On the first day of occupancy of a property, immediately check these essential aspects:
1. **Security deposit receipt**: Request a copy of the bank receipt confirming the deposit into a blocked account in your name. 2. Written contract: Keep a copy of the original contract with the date, landlord's signature, and all specific clauses. 3. Photographic attachments: Document the condition of the property with dated photos; immediately contest any pre-existing damages. 4. Meter readings: Record readings for electricity, gas, and water; request a written statement from the landlord. 5. Written communications: Keep all important communications in writing.
### Procedure for contesting rent
If the proposed rent seems excessive compared to the premises, property characteristics, and geographical area:
Day 1: Receive the contract and note the exact date of receipt. Days 2-30: Gather comparative data on similar rents in the area through online ads, local agencies, and cantonal databases. Days 25-30: Complete the appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority of Fribourg (form downloadable from the official website). Attach comparative documentation and state the reasons for the contestation. After the appeal: Wait for the summons to the conciliation office. It is not mandatory to be assisted by a lawyer. Decision: The authority communicates the outcome in writing within a period usually between 30 and 60 days. If favorable, the landlord is obliged to reduce the rent retroactively.
### Valid termination procedure
If the landlord communicates a termination:
1. Verify that the form is the official cantonal one (available at the Fribourg conciliation office). 2. Check the date of receipt, the original signature of the landlord, and the tenant's signature if required. 3. Calculate the notice period: first year = minimum 1 month; 2nd-9th year = 2 months; 10th year and beyond = 3 months from receipt. 4. If the termination does not comply with the form or federal terms, appeal to the conciliation authority within 30 days of receipt and request its annulment. 5. If the termination is correct, prepare to leave the property by the indicated date, possibly verifying the condition with the landlord.
Disputes over deposits, rents, and terminations are always first resolved by the cantonal conciliation authority of Fribourg. Only if dissatisfied with its verdict can one appeal to the cantonal civil court. Consult the official website of the Fribourg cantonal administration to find the competent office and download updated forms.

The termination of a lease agreement in the Canton of Fribourg must follow precise federal rules. The landlord wishing to terminate the contract is obliged to use the official cantonal form of Fribourg. This formality is mandatory: a notice of termination completed on a blank sheet, by email without the official document, or in any other format than the cantonal form is completely null and void and has no legal effect.
The notice of termination deadlines vary depending on the years of lease: - **First year of lease**: 1 month notice - Years 2-9 of lease: 2 months notice - From the tenth year of lease onwards: 3 months notice
These terms are set by federal law and apply regardless of what is written in the lease agreement. Clauses that provide for shorter deadlines are null; longer deadlines, however, remain valid if accepted in writing by both parties.
### How to obtain the official cantonal form of Fribourg
The official termination form for the Canton of Fribourg is available from the Fribourg cantonal administration. It can be downloaded from the official website of the Canton, obtained in paper format from the administrative offices, or by contacting the competent office by telephone to receive the updated document. Using the correct and current form is essential to ensure the legal validity of the notice of termination.
### Common errors in the termination procedure
Some terminations do not take effect because they are formally incorrect. The most frequent errors include: - Failure to use the official cantonal form (verbal termination or on personal paper) - Incorrect calculation of the notice period or the end date of the lease - Omission of data required by the form (tenant's name, address, landlord's data) - Failure to deliver the form to the recipient within the prescribed period (late delivery) - Absence of the landlord's handwritten signature on paper (if required by the cantonal procedure)
An invalid notice of termination has no legal effect, and the lease continues under the previous conditions. For this reason, it is always advisable to check with the cantonal conciliation authority whether the notice of termination has been correctly completed and notified before assuming that the lease has ended.
If you are a landlord renting a property in the Canton of Fribourg, remember that management and maintenance costs may be deductible from your taxes. Check out our [tax return calculator](nav:tax-return) to find out how to take advantage of these deductions and optimize your tax situation.
## Recommended tools For an updated estimate, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [CHF-EUR exchange comparator](nav:exchange). ## The conciliation authority in rental matters
The Canton of Fribourg has a specialized conciliation authority for rental disputes. This cantonal administrative body plays a crucial role in resolving conflicts between tenants and landlords, serving as an accessible filter before resorting to lengthy and costly judicial proceedings. The authority is staffed by experts in rental law and is familiar with the specificities of the local real estate market.
### When to resort to the conciliation authority
The conciliation authority is competent for disputes related to: - Rental fees deemed excessive or unfair - Unjustified or incorrectly returned security deposits - Interpretation of ambiguous contractual clauses - Validity of a notice (e.g., notice on correct or incorrect form) - Liability for damage to the leased property (who pays, how much) - Maintenance and repair obligations of the property (landlord vs tenant responsibility) - Right of occupation after the end of the contract
### The conciliation procedure: operational steps
The procedure is simple and accessible even to those without legal experience. The tenant or landlord submits a written appeal to the cantonal conciliation authority within the prescribed deadline (usually 30 days from the occurrence of the disputed fact). In the appeal, the facts, reasons for the dispute, and what is requested (rent reduction, deposit return, declaration of notice nullity, etc.) are described.
The authority receives the appeal, communicates it to the counterparty, and summons them to a conciliation meeting. During the meeting, both parties present their positions, and the authority, based on experience and regulations, attempts to facilitate an amicable agreement. If an agreement is reached, it is binding and ends the dispute without the need for judicial recourse.
### If conciliation does not lead to an agreement
If no agreement is reached during the conciliation attempt, the authority drafts a technical report with its evaluations and conclusions. This report serves as a legal basis for any subsequent judicial appeal. Although not binding like a judgment, the authority's report has legal weight and facilitates subsequent resolution in court.
### Concrete advantages of the conciliation procedure
Resorting to the conciliation authority presents tangible advantages: - Free or minimal cost procedure (no court fees) - Short resolution times (usually weeks, not months) - Rental experts who evaluate disputes according to clear criteria - Amicable solution that preserves the relationship between the parties - Alternative to lengthy, costly, and conflictual court proceedings - Legal documentation recognized even for possible subsequent appeal
### How to contact the Fribourg conciliation authority
To initiate a conciliation procedure or obtain preliminary information, it is necessary to contact the Fribourg cantonal administration directly. Contact details, reception hours, and forms for submitting the appeal are available on the official website of the Canton of Fribourg. It is possible to submit the appeal in person at the counters, by mail, or sometimes through cantonal electronic platforms.
If you have doubts about your rights as tenants or landlords in the Canton of Fribourg, contacting the conciliation authority is the first recommended step. The cantonal office provides clarifications on federal regulations (CO art. 253 ff.) and applicable local procedures without consultation costs.

item.title: Bag landing in chiaroscuro for Shein's fast fashion
item.description: Shein's IPO in Hong Kong on September 1 raised $1.75 billion but fell 10%. France introduces "malus" up to €19.50 on disposable fashion. Switzerland maintains less stringent rules.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Shein debuts in Hong Kong on September 1st: raises 1.75 billion USD, but initial 10% drop - France applies 'malus' up to 19.50 € per fast fashion item starting tomorrow - Switzerland maintains less stringent rules on online fast fashion - European tax on small packages (under 150 €) had already curbed imports
## Key facts - **What**: Shein's IPO in Hong Kong + new French tax on fast fashion - When: September 1st, 2026 (IPO); September 2nd, 2026 (French malus) - Where: Hong Kong for the IPO, France for the new surcharge, Switzerland for regulatory context - Who: Shein (Chinese giant), French Ministry of Ecological Transition, Minister Mathieu Lefèvre - IPO Amount: approximately 1.75 billion USD (13.6 billion HKD) - IPO Price: 48.56 Hong Kong dollars per share (~6.24 USD) - French Surcharge: up to 19.50 € per item by 2030
### Shein's Stock Market Debut Shein, the Chinese fast fashion giant, debuted on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange on Tuesday, September 1st, 2026, with mixed results. The company offered approximately 280 million shares at a price of 48.56 Hong Kong dollars per share (approximately 6.24 USD), raising a total of 13.6 billion Hong Kong dollars, equivalent to approximately 1.75 billion USD.
The notable figure is the drop on the first day of trading: the stock fell to 43.72 Hong Kong dollars (approximately 5.62 USD), a 10% decline from the offering price. The session closed at 48.50 Hong Kong dollars, with a 0.1% drop from the original IPO price.
Despite the negative debut, the operation allowed Shein to raise significant funds to continue its global expansion in the rapidly growing ultra-cheap fashion sector.
### The French Regulatory Response Parallel to Shein's stock market debut, France has intensified its regulatory approach to ultra-fast fashion and disposable goods. Starting Wednesday, September 2nd, 2026, Paris will apply a 'malus' (surcharge) on each fashion item that can reach up to 19.50 euros per item by 2030. A concrete example: an imported jacket could incur this surcharge.
The French Ministry of Ecological Transition stated that 'it is urgent to act quickly on fast fashion.' Officials also emphasized that 'the differences in scale are extremely significant' between the production of the Chinese giant Shein and traditional French fashion brands.
This regulatory move follows the implementation of the previous European tax on small packages (valued under 150 euros), which had already curbed the importation of very low-cost fast fashion items into the European territory. ## The Swiss competitive advantage
Switzerland, unlike France and other EU countries, maintains "less stringent" rules on imported fast fashion. This means that Swiss consumers will continue to find more competitive prices for online shopping of ultra-cheap fashion, at least in the short and medium term.
The new French "malus," which can exceed 19 euros per item by 2030, creates a significant cost differential in cross-border markets. A French consumer ordering from Shein or similar platforms would have to bear the tax surcharge, while a Swiss consumer — for now — would not. This competitive advantage keeps Switzerland as a relatively more affordable market for this segment.
### Effects on commercial traffic and imports
The European tax on small packages was already in effect before the new French "malus" and had already significantly slowed the flow of fast fashion orders to EU countries. The new French surcharge further aggravates this scenario, creating an even more advantageous commercial "shore" for Switzerland in the European context.
However, Shein's IPO — despite the initial 10% drop — testifies to the global importance and commercial strength of these ultra-cheap business models. The IPO allowed the Chinese giant to raise nearly 1.75 billion USD, confirming the vitality of this market segment.
### European trend towards environmental regulation
The European regulatory context suggests a growing and structural trend towards regulating fast fashion. If other European countries follow France's example in the coming years, Switzerland could find itself in a position of relative competitive advantage — but also under increasing political pressure to align with stricter environmental standards or to consider similar measures.
For now, European surcharges on fast fashion do not directly affect Swiss consumers, who remain in a market with less stringent regulation. This does not mean there are no environmental or social costs of fast fashion, but simply that there are no state-imposed tax surcharges in Switzerland yet.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## What to do as a Swiss consumer
### Check the total cost of online orders
As long as Switzerland maintains less stringent rules on fast fashion, online shopping remains competitive compared to neighboring European markets. However, it is crucial to check the total cost before completing the order:
**1. Import customs fees:** Although there is no specific Swiss "malus," imported goods from Shein or similar platforms are still subject to Swiss customs checks (import VAT and potential duties). Always check the final invoice summary with all costs included.
2. Cross-border taxes: The European "small package tax" system (goods under 150 euros) already affects the total cost for those ordering from European platforms. From September 2, the French "malus" is added to this picture. If a product crosses French territory during transit to other European countries, additional costs may apply.
### Compare prices and quality with local markets
Despite the price advantage of ultra-cheap online fashion, it is worth carefully comparing:
- Delivery times and platform reliability - Actual quality of materials (fast fashion has very short production cycles) - Costs and ease of returns and refunds - Availability of customer support in Italian or German
Using price comparison tools can help verify if the online savings really compensate for the added value of the local Swiss market in terms of quality, reliability, and delivery times.
### Convert currencies and estimate the total cost in CHF
In the case of purchases from Shein or similar platforms (which often quote in CNY — Chinese yuan — or USD), it is essential to use a [real-time currency exchange tool](nav:exchange) to verify the actual cost in Swiss francs before confirming the order. The exchange rate can vary significantly between the time of the displayed price and the actual payment.
### Follow the evolution of Swiss regulations
The French and European regulations suggest that Switzerland may also consider similar measures in the coming years, especially if environmental pressure on fast fashion increases. It is advisable to monitor the communications of the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) and the federal parliamentary debates regarding environmental policies and fashion sustainability.
Operational conclusion: Switzerland remains a less regulated market for online fast fashion. This advantage is temporary. Those who wish to take advantage of this competitive window should do so with awareness of the risks of returns, real delivery times, and actual quality. Before any significant order, use the [total cost calculator](nav:calculator) to include VAT, duties, and final fees.

item.title: Kindergarten Freiburg: childcare, costs
item.description: Child custody in the canton of Fribourg: rates, subsidies available and procedures for applying for cantonal contributions to families.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Childcare in Switzerland is a cantonal responsibility: daycare centers, day families, after-school care - Fees calculated based on family income and number of children; cantonal subsidies reduce costs - Childcare expenses are partially deductible from federal taxes
## Key facts - **What**: Childcare (daycare centers, day families, after-school care) is the responsibility of the cantons - When: Available from a few months old until school entry (3-4 years) - Where: Canton of Fribourg - Who: Cantonal and municipal administrations, private and public facilities - Amount: Fees vary by income; cantonal subsidies available
In the Canton of Fribourg, as in all of Switzerland, childcare during the day is a shared responsibility between families, public and private facilities, and cantonal support. There is no single federal system of public daycare centers: each canton regulates the offer, fees, and subsidies independently.
Childcare options include professional daycare centers (public and private), day families (family assistants who care for children in their homes), after-school care for children after kindergarten, and public vs. private communal facilities.
Fees and models vary significantly between cantons. Generally, they are calculated based on family income (with a progressive scale), the number of children in care, the number of days and weekly hours, and the type of facility (daycare center vs. day family). Each canton offers subsidies for families with incomes below defined thresholds to facilitate access.
### Childcare options in the Canton of Fribourg
Professional daycare centers are facilities managed by qualified educators, operated by municipal public entities or private managers. They care for children from a few months old up to 4-5 years, with structured educational programs and a regulated child-educator ratio.
Day families involve accredited assistants who care for children in their homes, with a maximum of 5 children at a time. They offer flexible hours and a family environment, often with lower fees compared to daycare centers.
After-school care facilities care for children after kindergarten or primary school, until 18-19. Often managed by municipalities or associations, they provide care, snacks, homework help, and recreational activities.
Many families choose based on criteria such as hours (full-time, 3-5 days, flexible), proximity to home or workplace, child-educator ratio, educational curriculum (Montessori, Reggio Emilia, public). Availability of spots is often limited: registrations should be made 6-12 months in advance. ### How fares are calculated
Rates for kindergarten and daycare in Switzerland follow standardized models. Most cantons use income brackets: the canton defines income brackets (e.g. CHF <60'000/year, CHF 60'000-80 '000, CHF 80' 000-100 '000, etc.), each with a different daily rate.
The basic daily rate varies depending on the property and canton. In addition, the cost can increase with additional hours (afternoon care, Wednesday afternoon, summer days, evenings), additional days beyond the standard ones, and extra services (specialized canteen, language courses, extracurricular activities).
Daytime family often has lower rates than professional kindergarten, since management costs are lower (less staff, no dedicated building). However, quality and certifications may vary.
### Cantonal subsidies and reductions
The Canton of Freiburg and the municipalities offer subsidies to mitigate the burden of costs on families. Subsidies are available for: - Families with income below defined threshold (specific amounts and thresholds vary by canton) - Siblings in simultaneous custody (progressive reduction: second child 20-30% discount, third even more) - Municipal public facilities (often rates already lower than private, with additional subsidies)
Subsidies are usually provided as: - Percentage reduction on the daily rate (e.g. 30% discount if income <CHF 70'000) - "Good service" that reduce
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to find facilities and obtain subsidies: step-by-step procedure
Step 1 – Identify available facilities Request a list of accredited public and private daycare centers from your municipality of residence. Many municipalities maintain online registers. Consult daycare center management associations (Swiss Daycare Center Association, Cantonal Federations). Check if municipalities offer online platforms for searching facilities. Visit candidate facilities, collect educational programs, schedules, contacts, and estimated waiting lists.
Step 2 – Apply for cantonal subsidy Submit a cantonal subsidy application to the competent municipal or cantonal office (ideal timing: 6-12 months before the start of care). Attach income certification: federal and cantonal tax returns for the last 2 years, sometimes an income certificate from the employer. Receive authorization/amount of subsidy in support of the enrollment application to the facility.
Step 3 – Enroll the child Contact the chosen facility, verify availability and timeline. Complete the official enrollment form. Attach required documentation (birth certificate, LAMal health insurance card, copies of parental authorizations if separated). Sign the contract specifying rates (gross and net rate with subsidy applied), schedules, cancellation conditions, responsibilities, and educational plans.
Step 4 – Documentation for tax deductibility Keep all monthly invoices from the facility (main document). Request a payment certificate or annual receipt from the facility. In the first year, attach a copy of the contract and monthly payment certificates. In subsequent years, only the annual payment receipt. Deductibility applies only if one of the parents declares the expense in the federal (IFD) and cantonal tax returns.
### Additional considerations: parental leave and health insurance Switzerland offers federal protection for parental leave, funded by the IPG system (Loss of Earnings Compensation). The mother is entitled to 14 weeks of paid leave at 80% of her salary. The father is entitled to 2 weeks at 80%. Many cantons and private companies offer more generous additional leave.
Additionally, every child residing in Switzerland must be insured with a health insurance fund (LAMal/KVG) within 3 months of birth or arrival. The costs of premiums vary by canton, region, and age (children have lower premiums than adults). Cantonal health subsidies can cover part of the premiums for low-income families.
**Start now**: Contact your municipality of residence to receive the list of facilities and the cantonal subsidy application form. With planning 6-12 months in advance, you ensure availability and optimal subsidies. [Use our calculator to estimate care costs based on your income and family.](nav:calculator)

item.title: Apprenticeship in the Canton of Fribourg: practical guide
item.description: How to find an internship, sign the contract, know your rights and salary. The complete guide to the Swiss vocational training system in the Canton of Fribourg.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Apprenticeship in Switzerland follows the EFA (Federal Vocational Education and Training Certificate) system, recognized nationally - Training lasts 3–4 years and combines practical business experience (70–80%) with vocational school lessons (20–30%) - A written contract is mandatory and regulates rights, duties, salary, and hours
## Key facts - **System**: EFA — dual training with federal recognition - Duration: 3–4 years depending on the profession - Territory: Entire Switzerland, including Canton Fribourg - Mode: Practical training in the company + lessons in vocational school - Certificate: Valid throughout Switzerland and internationally recognized
Apprenticeship in Canton Fribourg follows the national Swiss vocational training system, one of the most appreciated in Europe. It is not a regular school nor a standard job: it is a dual path that combines concrete business practice and theoretical training in vocational school.
Those who complete an apprenticeship obtain the EFA (Federal Vocational Education and Training Certificate), a certificate valid throughout Switzerland and internationally recognized. Canton Fribourg fully participates in this national system.
### How is the training structured
Apprentices spend about 70–80% of their time in the company (applied practice) and 20–30% in vocational school (theoretical lessons). This balance allows for the acquisition of concrete skills in the field while being trained in the fundamentals of the chosen profession.
The duration varies according to the qualification: most apprenticeships last 3 years, some require 4. Throughout the entire path, the apprentice remains an employee of the company with a written contract that regulates mutual obligations, hours, and remuneration.
### Where to look for an apprenticeship position
The search begins with a conscious choice: which profession is of interest? Opportunities range from technical and craft sectors (mechanics, plumbing, electricity, carpentry, construction) to administrative, commercial, healthcare, hospitality, and agricultural sectors.
The main channels for finding a position are: - Online portals for [job ads](nav:jobs): Federal and cantonal platforms collect job postings from companies looking for apprentices. Searching by region and sector facilitates orientation. - Direct contacts: Requesting information from local companies, especially in sectors widespread in the Fribourg territory. - School guidance offices: Canton institutions provide addresses, advice, and support in the application process. - Fairs and information days: Local events where companies present their apprenticeship programs. - Informational interviews: Meeting professionals helps clarify one's inclinations and the realities of the job.
It is essential to apply in advance: many companies decide on their apprentices 12–24 months before the start of the program. ### The apprenticeship contract: rights and duties
Once you have found an employer, the first formal act is the signing of the **apprenticeship contract**. This binding document must be written and is mandatory under federal labor law.
The contract clearly specifies:
- The profession and the field of activity - The start date and the expected duration - The gross monthly salary (or hourly rate) - Working hours and mandatory breaks - The rights and duties of both parties - The probation and notice periods
The apprentice has specific rights: they cannot be exploited or assigned to dangerous tasks without adequate supervision. They are entitled to a safe working environment, regular breaks, and to attend vocational school without loss of salary.
In turn, the apprentice commits to learning diligently, respecting working hours, following the instructions of the company trainer, and actively participating in school lessons.
### Apprentice's remuneration
Remuneration is one of the most important aspects. In Switzerland, the apprentice's salary is lower than that of a qualified worker — this is normal and consistent with the fact that the apprentice is still learning the trade.
Switzerland does not have a uniform federal minimum wage for apprentices. However, the Canton of Fribourg, like other cantons, sets cantonal minimums for certain professions or sectors. These vary according to the field (trade, craft, industry, services) and the year of apprenticeship.
In practice: - The first year provides a lower monthly salary. - In the second and third year, the pay gradually increases. - Towards the end of the training, the remuneration approaches that of a qualified worker but remains slightly lower.
All taxes and social contributions (AVS/AI, unemployment insurance, accident insurance) are deducted from the gross salary, exactly as for any other employee. The apprentice pays a share of pension contributions equal to 5.3% of the salary, while the employer contributes the corresponding amount.
Consult your [pay slip](nav:payslip) to understand how deductions are calculated. It is essential to read the contract carefully before signing: it must contain a clear indication of the gross salary and the payment method (monthly, bi-weekly, etc.).
### Duration and working hours
The maximum working hours for an apprentice follow federal labor rules: up to 45 hours per week in sectors such as industry, offices, and trade, and up to 50 hours in other sectors (agriculture, livestock farming). In practice, many apprentices work 40–42 hours per week.
Vacations: the apprentice is entitled to a minimum of 4 weeks of vacation per year (20 working days). If you are under 20 years old, the right increases to 5 weeks (25 days). Vacations should be agreed with the employer, preferably during school holidays, to avoid conflicts with lessons.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Step-by-step procedure: how to apply
Step 1: Orientation and career choice Before looking for an employer, clarify which sector truly attracts you. Cantonal orientation offices provide free advice. It is useful to visit companies, meet professionals, understand the daily work and career prospects.
**Step 2: Active search** Use online portals, send spontaneous applications, participate in vocational fairs. The ideal search starts 12–18 months before the date you want to start.
Step 3: Interview and selection The employer will conduct interviews and, possibly, practical tests to assess aptitude, motivation, and compatibility with the company. It is an opportunity to ask questions and understand the work environment concretely.
Step 4: Contract signing Once accepted, the contract is signed by both parties. It contains all the details (start date, duration, gross salary, hours, employer, and apprentice). One copy remains with the apprentice, another with the employer; a third can be deposited with the competent cantonal office.
Step 5: Enrollment in vocational school The Canton of Fribourg coordinates the enrollment of apprentices in the appropriate vocational schools. The employer usually supports this administrative procedure. School starts in sync with the apprenticeship start date.
Step 6: Training and balance From this moment, the dual path begins: practice in the company according to the weekly schedule (usually 4 days) and lessons in vocational school (1–2 days).
### Professional Maturity: the next step Many apprentices, once they have completed their VET, continue towards professional maturity (PM). This is an additional diploma that allows access to universities of applied sciences (UAS) and certain programs of traditional universities.
Professional maturity involves additional lessons in subjects such as languages, mathematics, social sciences, and a specialization related to the profession. It can be attended: - Integrated: during the last 1–2 years of the apprenticeship (full-time or part-time) - Subsequent: after completing the VET, in 1–2 additional years
In the Canton of Fribourg, vocational schools and training centers offer both paths.
### Final practical points Some important details before starting:
- Trial period: The first months (usually 1–3 months) are considered a trial period, during which both parties can terminate with short notice. - Health insurance: The apprentice must be insured with a health insurance fund within 3 months from the start (mandatory for all residents). - Documentation: Keep the original contract, pay slips, and school attendance certificates. - Difficulties: If problems arise at work or school, cantonal mediation services are available to help resolve conflicts.
Explore the [companies that hire](nav:companies) in your sector to understand local realities.
Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) to simulate the net based on the gross amounts that will be offered to you, including all federal and cantonal deductions.
Apprenticeship in the Canton of Fribourg is a concrete investment in your future: it requires commitment and dedication but provides nationally and internationally recognized practical skills that open doors in the Swiss job market and beyond.

item.title: Permit L Freiburg: validity and extension
item.description: The short-term L permit allows foreigners to work in Switzerland for up to 1 year. Learn about extension rules, employer constraints, and how to switch to B and C permits.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The L permit allows you to work in Switzerland for a maximum of 1 year - Extension is possible but depends on federal criteria and job availability - The permit is specifically tied to the employer and professional sector
## Key facts - **What**: Short-term permit for foreign workers - Maximum duration: 1 year - Scope: Canton of Fribourg (federal SEM system) - Managed by: State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level - Main restriction: Tied to the specific employer indicated in the permit
The short-term L permit is the regulatory tool through which Switzerland authorizes foreign workers to engage in dependent professional activities within the national territory. Managed by the State Secretariat for Migration (SEM) at the federal level, the L permit applies identically across all Swiss cantons, including the Canton of Fribourg, without additional authorizations from the cantonal administration beyond those stipulated by federal regulations.
### Maximum duration of the L permit
According to federal regulations, the L permit has a maximum validity of 1 year. This means that the foreign worker can reside and work in Switzerland for a period not exceeding 12 months from the date of issuance. Unlike residence (B) or settlement (C) permits, the L permit does not offer long-term stay and requires an explicit extension if the employment relationship continues beyond the initial term.
The L permit is specifically named after the employer: this means that the worker cannot change jobs without a formal modification to the permit itself. If the employment relationship ends before the expiration date, the permit automatically lapses, and the worker must leave the national territory or apply for a new permit for a new job position. This restriction reflects the objective of Swiss migration policy to anchor the permit to the actual economic need of the employer.
The procedure for obtaining the L permit begins before the foreigner's arrival in Switzerland. The employer submits the application to the competent cantonal office in Fribourg, attaching the employment contract, the candidate's identity documents, and sometimes professional qualification certificates. Once authorized, the permit allows entry and commencement of work activities according to the modalities specified in the document. ### Conditions of extension and constraints with the employer
The extension of the L permit is not automatic. When the permit is about to expire within 12 months of initial validity, the employer must submit a new application for renewal to the competent cantonal office. The extension is granted on the condition that the economic and working conditions justifying the initial authorisation still exist. item.title: Legumes with meat textures: ETH Zurich research
item.description: ETH researchers transform peas, beans and lentils into products with a fibrous meat-like structure, reducing food waste.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - ETH Zurich researchers transform legumes into fibrous structure similar to meat. - The method reduces food waste while preserving nutritional value. - Simple process: soaking, pureeing, heating, freezing the mass. - Applicable also in domestic kitchens; recipes developed by professional chefs.
## Key facts - **What**: Transformation of legumes (peas, beans, lentils) into products with fibrous texture - Who: Researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich (ETH), coordinated by Patrick Rühs - Where: ETH Zurich laboratories - How: Soaking legumes → pureeing → heating → freezing to create oriented lamellae - Why: Reduce food waste in industrial processes and preserve nutritional value - Legumes: Peas, beans and lentils (96% of world production) - When: Study published in the specialized journal "NJP Science of Food" - Application: Simple method replicable also in domestic kitchens
The Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich has developed an innovative process to transform common legumes — peas, beans and lentils — into products with a fibrous consistency comparable to that of meat. The announcement comes directly from the Zurich researchers, who primarily aim to reduce food waste in the food production sector.
In contemporary industrial production, raw materials are frequently decomposed into their essential components: proteins, starch and fats are separated and then recombined to create new products. During this process, a significant portion of the raw material is not utilized, generating considerable losses. The new method developed at ETH allows legumes to be transformed without losses into a food with an oriented and fibrous structure, maintaining the original nutritional value intact.
"A fibrous structure provides, during chewing, a sensation that many people appreciate in meat and fish," explains Professor Patrick Rühs in an official statement from the institution. "In meat or fish, this fibrous structure is the result of the arrangement of muscle fibers," adds the researcher, highlighting how the new process artificially reproduces the same effect.
### The transformation process
The methodology is surprisingly straightforward. The researchers initially soaked the legumes in water, then reduced them to a puree. Subsequently, this puree is heated until it acquires a gelatinous appearance. The crucial step is the freezing of the mass: during this stage, oriented lamellar structures are formed in the same direction. Once thawed, the product maintains this fibrous configuration stably.
Tests involved various varieties of beans, peas and lentils. The researchers observed variations in the final consistencies depending on the variety and water content. For example, red lentils produced a more compact structure compared to soybeans. "Our process works with a wide range of legumes, which represent 96% of world production," emphasizes Patrick Rühs.
### Simplicity of application and development prospects
A particularly relevant aspect of the new method is its accessibility: "The new method is so simple that anyone can apply it without problems in their own kitchen," says doctoral student Andrea Bach, directly involved in the research. This feature distinguishes it from complex industrial processes and makes it potentially usable by domestic consumers.
The ETH study was published in the specialized journal "NJP Science of Food," providing a solid scientific basis for the results. As a continuation of the project, the researchers intend to examine more closely how to control and modulate the different final consistencies of the product. The development of concrete recipes has been entrusted to professional chefs, indicating an interest in the practical culinary application of the method. ### Impact on sustainability and the Swiss food industry
The ETH research fits into an international context of growing attention to reducing food waste. According to UST (Federal Statistical Office) data, the Swiss food industry generates significant losses during industrial processing. This new method represents a concrete step towards optimizing production processes while simultaneously preserving the nutritional profile of foods.
The Swiss food industry, characterized by high quality standards, could directly benefit from this innovation. Legumes are relatively inexpensive raw materials, and transforming them into products with sensory properties comparable to meat could open interesting market segments, both for domestic consumption and export. Although Switzerland is not a major legume producer, it imports significant quantities from various regions of the world, particularly Europe and North Africa.
### Implications for the cost of living and legume prices
In the current context of attention to the [cost of living in Switzerland](nav:cost-of-living), the economic accessibility of legumes is a relevant factor. Legumes are low-cost plant proteins compared to meat, and improvements in processing could further reduce consumer prices. This is particularly significant for those living in cantons with higher costs of living, such as Zurich and Basel-City.
The VAT on food in Switzerland is set at 2.5% for foodstuffs, the lowest among standard rates. If legumes processed according to the new method enter the market as a shelf product, they will benefit from the same favorable taxation, maintaining competitive prices for consumers. Additionally, by reducing waste in the industrial production phase, producers could pass on part of these savings to Swiss consumers.
### Transition to mindful diets
The global trend towards plant-based diets is also growing in Switzerland. Legumes, rich in proteins and fibers, are increasingly considered valid alternatives to animal proteins. The new ETH process does not require complex chemical additives and works with 100% of the raw material, making it particularly attractive from a sustainability perspective.
Sensory perception remains a crucial factor: many consumers still choose meat because they appreciate the characteristic fibrous texture. If processed legumes could replicate this chewing sensation, they could win over a segment of consumers previously reluctant to plant proteins. In the long term, innovations of this type contribute to stabilizing the prices of plant proteins in the Swiss market, reducing dependence on meat imports and promoting a more mindful food transition.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ### How to replicate the method at home
For those who wish to experiment with the new process in their home kitchen, the procedure is accessible and does not require specialized equipment. Here are the essential steps to obtain legumes with a fibrous consistency.
**Step 1 - Preparation**: Take dry legumes (red lentils, common beans, dried peas) and soak them in cold water for at least 8-12 hours. This step is crucial to soften the legumes and facilitate the subsequent transformation.
Step 2 - Reduction to puree: After soaking, drain the legumes and reduce them to a puree using a blender or food processor. The final consistency should be homogeneous, similar to a thick mashed potato compound.
Step 3 - Gelatinous heating: Transfer the puree to a pot and heat it over moderate heat, stirring continuously. This phase serves to evaporate some of the water and give the mass a gelatinous appearance. The time required depends on the amount and initial water content, but generally 15-20 minutes are sufficient.
Step 4 - Freezing: Once the desired consistency is reached, transfer the mass to a container suitable for freezing (tray or jar) and place in the freezer for at least 24 hours. During this phase, the lamellar structures that will give the final fibrous texture are formed.
Step 5 - Thawing and use: Remove the product from the freezer and let it thaw at room temperature or in the refrigerator. Once thawed, it will retain the oriented fibrous structure. The product can be used as a base for vegetable meatballs, burgers, legume ragù, or other dishes that require a hearty texture.
### Choosing the most suitable legumes
Not all legumes will produce the same consistency. According to ETH research data, red lentils generate a more compact texture, while other legumes such as soybeans produce slightly more crumbly structures. It is recommended to start with red lentils or red beans, both easily available in Swiss grocery stores and specialized organic markets.
### Obtaining Swiss legumes and employment in the sector
Although Switzerland is not among the world's leading legume producers, several cantons (particularly Vaud, Fribourg, and Geneva) cultivate modest amounts of organic legumes. To support local production and reduce the carbon footprint, it is advisable to check with local farmers' markets, cantonal agricultural cooperatives, and certified organic product stores for the availability of legumes grown in Switzerland. The development of recipes is entrusted to professionals in the culinary sector, highlighting how food innovation generates qualified employment in Switzerland.

ETH research continues to develop new formulations and refine the control of consistencies. item.title: L Fribourg permit: duration and renewal
item.description: L Freiburg permit: valid for up to 1 year, renewal and transition to B and C permits. Procedures, documents and employer constraints.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The L permit is valid for up to 1 year and is intended for temporary work in Switzerland - It is renewable upon joint request with the employer, under the same conditions - From the L permit you pass to B (residence, 5 years) and then to C (residence, 10 years)
## Key Facts - **What**: Residence permit and temporary work for foreigners in Switzerland - Duration: Up to 1 year (not automatically renewable; renewal on request) - Where: Canton of Fribourg (federal SEM regulations for all cantons) - Who: Secrétariat d'État aux migrations (SEM) — federal competence; cantonal administration by cantonal procedure - Local authority: Office of Employment and Migration of the Canton of Fribourg
### What is the L permit and how does it work
The short-term L permit is the instrument through which Switzerland regulates the temporary entry of foreign workers. It is valid for a maximum of 12 months and allows you to live and work in the country during this period. Unlike other permits (B for residence, C for domicile), the L permit does not offer long-term stability, but is an ideal solution for temporary, seasonal or project-specific assignments.
In the canton of Fribourg, as in all other Swiss cantons, the L permit is subject to the federal regulation of the Secrétariat d'État aux migrations. There are no specific cantonal variants that differentiate the conditions in Fribourg from other cantons: the rules on duration, renewal and contractual obligations remain uniform at the national level. The cantonal administrative procedure, however, is handled by the office of the canton of Fribourg responsible for employment and immigration.
### Who can get it and employer constraints
The L permit is subject to the submission of a genuine job offer. The Swiss employer (or the Swiss branch of a foreign company) must prove that it cannot find a resource available on the domestic market and that the position is actually necessary. This check is carried out by the competent authorities when submitting the application.
The employer remains the real "anchor" of the permit: the L permit is nominative, i.e. in the name of a specific company, and the worker cannot change employer without the re-registration procedure and new approval by the SEM and the canton. This is a fundamental constraint that distinguishes the L permit from the simple authorization to reside. It means that the permit is linked to the permanence in the same workplace and that any change requires timely notification to the authorities. ### Renewal of the L permit and conditions for extension
An L permit can be renewed, but renewal is not automatic. The procedure requires a new joint application by the employer and the foreigner to the Fribourg cantonal administration, preferably submitted 60-90 days before expiry. Renewal is possible if the initial conditions are still met: the employer confirms the employment need, the employment is real and continues, and there are no legal impediments such as no criminal record, tax regularity, and timely payment of social contributions (AHV/IV, unemployment insurance, health insurance).
The duration of each renewal period is still up to 1 year. There is no theoretical limit to the number of consecutive renewals, as long as the conditions remain met. However, the Swiss permit system is designed to incentivize temporariness: if the employment becomes structural and permanent, it is more convenient for everyone (employer, employee, cantonal authority) to transition to a B (residence) permit, which offers a validity of 5 years and less administrative bureaucracy.
### Transition from L to B: when and how
After the first year of the L permit (or after one or more consecutive renewals), the transition to the B permit is the natural step. The B permit is valid for 5 years and can be renewed indefinitely, representing significantly greater stability. To access the B permit, there is no need to change cantons: the canton of Fribourg remains the competent party. The administrative procedure is handled by the Fribourg office, which automatically assesses the possibility of transition once the first L permit has expired and if the requirements are met.
Minimum requirements for the transition to B include: documented actual employment for at least 1 year (demonstrable with payslips, renewed contracts); absence of pending sanctions or expulsion measures; regular and full payment of social contributions; ability to economic self-sufficiency, demonstrated by the net income that allows you to live without cantonal public support.
### Difference Between B and C Permit
The C permit (domicile) represents the final step in the progression. It is generally available after 10 years of continuous legal residence (or 5 years for citizens of the European Union or the European Economic Area), and offers almost absolute stability. Unlike the B permit, the C permit allows for wider job mobility: it is possible to change employer and sector with fewer administrative constraints and without the need for a new authorization for each change.
In addition, the C permit is a prerequisite for accessing ordinary Swiss naturalization, which then requires the C permit plus 10 years of actual residence, together with the requirements established by the canton and municipality of residence.

The renewal procedure is managed by the Fribourg cantonal administration. Here are the operational steps:
Step 1 — Coordination with the employer (60-90 days before expiration): The employer and the employee must agree on the willingness to renew. It is essential that the employer confirms in writing the stable employment and the need to continue employment beyond the expiration date of the current permit.
Step 2 — Collection of documentation: the employer prepares a reasoned declaration (explaining the reasons for continuing), the renewed or extended employment contract, the worker's last 3 pay slips, a copy of the company's tax return for the last 2 financial years, and (if the employee has resided in Switzerland for more than 2 years) a certificate of good conduct.
Step 3 — Submission of the application: joint application (employer + employee, preferably with both signatures certified) to the competent office in the canton of Fribourg (usually the employment or migration desk). Check whether the canton accepts digital applications via the SEM platform or whether it requires paper documentation.
Step 4 — Verification and timing: The canton of Fribourg takes an average of 4-8 weeks to evaluate the application. It is not mandatory for the permit to be renewed BEFORE it expires (the employee can take advantage of a short tolérance during the verification procedure), but it is advisable to submit the application in time to avoid interruptions.
Step 5 — Issuance and Communication: Once approved, the positive decision is notified to both the employer and the employee. The renewed permit is valid for an additional 12 months from the date of approval.
### Documents required for renewal
- Valid passport and photocopy of personal page - Renewed or extended employment contract (with signature of both parties) - Last 3 pay slips (payslip) - Company tax return (last 2 tax years) - Certificate of good conduct (if resident for more than 2 years) - Statement of account from the provident fund (AHV/IV) to check the regularity of contributions
### When it is convenient to switch from permission L to B
If the renewal of the L permit becomes recurrent (more than 2 consecutive renewals, i.e. more than 3 years of stay), it is advisable to consider switching to B. Concrete advantages: less bureaucracy (renewal every 5 years instead of every year); expanded labor mobility (possibility of changing employer with a simplified procedure); recognition of stable and long-term residence, with tax and social security benefits.
Conversely, if the occupation is actually temporary (maximum 2-3 years), the L permit remains the most pragmatic choice: less administrative effort, and no obligation to transition to B.
### Support and practical tools
Further information on cantonal specific procedures and application forms can be found on the official website of the administration of the canton of Fribourg (www.fr.ch, Employment and Migration section).

## In brief - ARE hearing for adaptation of the wind energy concept from 1 September 2026 - Procedure open to cantons and public participation nationwide - Objective: to strengthen planning and increase the construction of wind farms - Required to align with new legal provisions and regulatory bases
## Key Facts - **What**: Adaptation of Switzerland's Wind Energy Concept - When: 1 September 2026 (start date of the hearing) - Where: Switzerland (federal procedure involving cantons) - Who: Federal Office for Spatial Development (ARE) - Type of procedure: Hearing of the cantons + public participation - Purpose: To adapt the Conception to new legal provisions and new regulatory bases - Expected result: Strengthen planning security for authorities and managers; increase the probability of new wind farms being built
On 1 September 2026, the Federal Office for Spatial Development (ARE) initiated the hearing of the cantons and public participation to adapt Switzerland's Wind Energy Concept. The procedure is necessary to incorporate the new legal provisions and new foundations that have characterized recent regulatory developments in the energy sector. The adaptation is not just a technical revision: it aims to strengthen the security of spatial planning for local authorities and wind project managers, and at the same time to concretely increase the chances of new wind farms being built on Swiss territory.
### What is the Wind Energy Conception
The Wind Energy Concept is a federal planning instrument that defines the principles and criteria for the establishment of wind farms on Swiss territory. It provides the framework for cantons, municipalities and project promoters to identify suitable areas for the construction of wind turbines, balancing energy needs, landscape protection and environmental considerations. This instrument reflects the federal competence in spatial planning and national energy strategy, while remaining subject to coordination with specific cantonal policies. The periodic adaptation of the Concept ensures that the instrument remains consistent with the evolution of energy and spatial legislation. ### Why Adjustment Is Necessary
The adaptation of the Wind Energy Concept stems from the need to align the instrument with the new legal provisions recently introduced in the Swiss regulatory framework. The ARE communication points out that the change was made necessary by the change in the legal bases governing wind energy. Although the source does not specify the individual amended laws, it is clear that the federal legislator considered it essential to update the procedural and substantive framework to ensure regulatory consistency.
The hearing procedure is the lever through which the federal government involves local institutions and civil society in the decision-making process. The cantons, which have significant autonomy in spatial planning, will be able to provide feedback on the adaptation based on their specific energy and spatial needs. Public participation, simultaneous with the cantonal hearing, allows citizens, interested bodies and project managers to express opinions and observations that will be evaluated by the ARE before the final version of the Conception.
### Implications for cantonal planning
Enhanced planning security means that authorities and promoters will have a clearer and more predictable tool when defining where to build wind farms. Less regulatory ambiguity translates into faster permitting times, reduced legal risks and increased investor confidence in the domestic wind sector. On the other hand, the objective of increasing the likelihood of new wind farms being built signals that the ARE has recognised the need to simplify or facilitate the deployment of wind turbines, probably in response to the national energy strategy that aims to increase the share of renewable energy in electricity generation. The cantons participating in the hearing will have the opportunity to negotiate the boundaries and criteria of the Conception to adapt them to the local territory, avoiding future conflicts between federal planning and cantonal decisions.

item.title: Swiss mobile telephony: Comcom excludes new providers
item.description: The Swiss Federal Communications Commission states: Economic and regulatory barriers make it virtually impossible for new competitors to enter the mobile phone market.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Comcom excludes new entrants: insurmountable economic and regulatory hurdles - Minimum cost: CHF 500 million to build your own network - Three current operators (Swisscom, Salt, Sunrise) will remain dominant - By 2033: Starlink should also build terrestrial networks in Switzerland
## Key Facts - **What**: Comcom declares it impossible for new competitors to enter mobile telephony - When: Statements by President Martin Bürki on Tuesday on the sidelines of the press conference - Where: Switzerland, national mobile market - Who: Federal Communications Commission (Comcom); current providers: Swisscom, Salt, Sunrise - Minimum amount: CHF 500 million to build own network - Deadline: 2033 to reach coverage of 50% of the population
The Swiss Federal Communications Commission (Comcom) does not foresee the entry of new players into the mobile phone market. President Martin Bürki confirmed on Tuesday, on the sidelines of a press conference in Bern in talks with the AWP news agency, that the economic and regulatory obstacles are simply too high for any competitor.
The construction of its own mobile network would cost, according to a rough estimate, at least half a billion Swiss francs. To this figure must be added the costs of setting up a sales and management organization in Switzerland. The difficulties do not end there: the new entrant would have to meet the minimum coverage requirement of 50% of the population.
### Regulatory and geographical walls that stop new entrants
Finding suitable spaces to install antennas is a second almost insurmountable obstacle. In Swiss cities, it is already very difficult to locate new antenna sites. In addition, there are restrictions imposed by the Federal Radiation Protection Regulation (NISV), which further limit the possible placement of infrastructure.
Comcom member Jean Christophe Schwaab stressed during the press conference that the commission would check very carefully whether a new entrant would be able to operate a mobile network covering half of the population by 2033. "A new entrant has to prove that it is technically and financially capable of doing this," he said.
This obligation would also apply to satellite operators such as Elon Musk's Starlink: they would also have to build their own terrestrial network, as satellite-only coverage does not meet Swiss requirements. According to Bürki, satellite-only coverage would only affect limited areas and cause interference in border regions. The auctioned frequencies are also not intended for the use of satellite communication.
As a result, it is very unlikely that a fourth bidder will appear at the next frequency auction in addition to the current operators Swisscom, Salt and Sunrise. ## How Comcom balances competition between three operators
Comcom, however, does not want a completely closed market. President Bürki said he wanted to maintain "three strong players in the market, which ultimately guarantee a good customer experience." The goal is to maintain functional competition between the three incumbents, avoiding scenarios in which one is the clear winner and one is the clear loser.
To achieve this balance, Comcom has introduced bidding constraints in the upcoming mobile frequency auction. According to Bürki, "we have tried to eliminate this risk."
### Spectrum limits: the new regulatory strategy
Bidding restrictions have been significantly tightened compared to the past. A single operator can purchase a maximum of 230 megahertz (MHz) of spectrum, which corresponds to around 43% of all available frequencies. In the previous auction in 2012, the upper limit was 270 MHz, or 50% of the total spectrum.
In addition to the general limit, Comcom has introduced specific restrictions for each frequency band, a measure that was absent from the 2012 auction:
- **Low band (800–900 MHz)**: a single bidder can be awarded a maximum of 38% of the available frequencies - Mid-band (1800–2100 MHz): the upper limit is set at two-thirds of the spectrum of that band - High-band (2600 MHz FDD): the limit rises to 71% of the available frequencies
These constraints aim to distribute the spectrum in a more balanced way among the three operators, preventing one of them from accumulating excessive market power. The regulatory model reflects a conscious choice by Comcom: to accept a stable oligopoly of three strong operators rather than risk a competitive war that could damage the national infrastructure.
### Regulatory stability versus new competition
The combination of structural economic barriers (the CHF 500 million for the initial infrastructure) and regulatory constraints makes the Swiss mobile market de facto closed to new entrants. Consumers will continue to choose between Swisscom, Salt and Sunrise, with competition regulated by Comcom rather than organic market forces. This approach sacrifices market openness in favour of infrastructure stability and the guarantee of widespread territorial coverage.

The closure of the market to new competitors has direct implications for Swiss residents and employees. On the one hand, they will not see the emergence of alternative operators that could offer more aggressive tariffs or innovative services. On the other hand, Comcom aims to prevent excessive power concentrations that would marginalize some operators, thus ensuring a choice between three stable and reliable providers.
Those who want to switch mobile providers in the coming years will choose between Swisscom, Salt and Sunrise, based on price, geographical coverage, mobile internet speed and quality of customer service. No new global competitors will emerge to disturb this balance in the medium term.
### Deadline 2033: Comcom's benchmark
The deadline by 2033 to reach 50% population coverage is a key milestone in Comcom's strategy. This is the benchmark that the committee will use to assess whether a hypothetical new entrant can legally operate in Switzerland. So far, no entity has expressed any intention to present itself as a new candidate for the next frequency auctions.
### How to monitor Comcom's decisions
If you wish to follow the development of the Swiss mobile market, you can consult Comcom's public documents on the official federal website. Spectrum auctions are public procedures: the results, winners and frequencies awarded are officially announced. Comcom will continue to monitor whether the three operators are meeting their territorial coverage and infrastructure investment commitments. Consumers who find mobile phone prices excessive can report their concerns to Comcom, which has regulatory tools to intervene in the event of anti-competitive behaviour.
